questions.prompt: A reset is in `@layer reset`; a normal unlayered component rule conflicts with it. Which normally wins?

options.text: The unlayered declaration
The reset-layer declaration regardless of order
The declaration with the shorter property name
The one with more whitespace

questions.explanation: Normal unlayered author declarations outrank normal declarations in named layers before specificity is compared.

questions.prompt: What is a useful reason to put low-priority defaults inside `:where()`?

options.text: It makes the selector match only visible elements
They remain easy for component rules to override due to zero specificity
It raises every nested selector's specificity
It disables inheritance

questions.explanation: `:where()` contributes zero specificity, which helps keep broad defaults easy to override.

questions.prompt: Which statements about normal declarations in cascade layers are correct?

options.text: Later declared layers outrank earlier layers.
Normal unlayered declarations outrank normal layered declarations.
Specificity is considered after layer priority.
A larger z-index changes cascade layer priority.

questions.explanation: Layer priority participates in the cascade before specificity; z-index is unrelated to declaration priority.

questions.prompt: What relationship does `:has()` let a selector test?

options.text: The network status of the stylesheet
The number of declarations in a rule
Whether a relative selector matches in relation to that element
Whether an element has a particular computed color

questions.explanation: `:has()` matches an element based on whether its relative selector argument matches within the relevant relationship.

questions.prompt: Match each cascade problem to the most relevant diagnostic.

rows.label: Third-party defaults are hard to override

columns.label: Inspect winning declaration and cascade criteria
Reduce selector weight or simplify contract

questions.explanation: Computed styles reveal the winner; specificity and layers address different sources of override pressure.

questions.prompt: Why should a component stylesheet avoid a selector that chains IDs, classes, and ancestors for ordinary styling?

options.text: Browsers cannot parse compound selectors
The selector automatically downloads more fonts
It prevents the cascade from running
Its high specificity makes later overrides and reuse harder

questions.explanation: Overly specific selectors create override pressure and make components harder to compose.

questions.prompt: A custom property contains the token `not-a-color`; `color: var(--ink, black)` is invalid. Why may `black` not be used?

options.text: The variable exists, but its substituted value is invalid for `color`; the fallback is not a general type checker
Fallbacks are ignored in every `var()` function
The `color` property never accepts named colors
Custom properties cannot be used in declarations

questions.explanation: The `var()` fallback handles an unavailable/invalid custom property, not arbitrary type errors after substitution.

questions.prompt: Which are sound design-token practices?

options.text: Expose every token as a global ID selector.
Use names that express a design role.
Centralize values used across components.
Allow scoped overrides for themes when needed.

questions.explanation: Semantic custom properties make design decisions reusable and themeable without relying on selector IDs.

questions.prompt: Why define a layer order once near the start of an application stylesheet?

options.text: It guarantees every browser downloads layers in parallel
It makes the priority relationship between style categories explicit
It eliminates the need for selectors
It changes the DOM order

questions.explanation: A declared layer order documents and stabilizes the cascade architecture across files.

questions.prompt: A user enables reduced motion in system settings. Which feature exposes that preference to CSS?

options.text: `prefers-contrast` only
`pointer`
`prefers-reduced-motion`
`resolution`

questions.explanation: The `prefers-reduced-motion` media feature reflects a user's motion preference.

questions.prompt: Match each CSS feature to a resilience strategy.

columns.label: Provide a safe `var()` fallback where appropriate
Adapt to viewport or user environment

questions.explanation: Use feature queries for support, value fallbacks for missing tokens, and media queries for environment conditions.

questions.prompt: Why is a visible `:focus-visible` outline preferable to removing outlines globally?

options.text: Outlines increase selector specificity
Browsers cannot draw borders on buttons
Focus styles only affect print
Keyboard users need a clear indication of the focused control

questions.explanation: A visible focus indicator communicates keyboard position; style it rather than removing the indicator without replacement.

questions.prompt: Which CSS approach is safest for meaningful text that must also be available to assistive technology?

options.text: Put the text in the document, not only in `::before` content
Generate the only copy with `content`
Render it as a background image
Hide it with `display: none`

questions.explanation: Generated content is not a dependable replacement for meaningful document text; keep essential content in HTML.

questions.prompt: Which checks are useful when validating responsive CSS?

options.text: Test a narrow viewport and a wide viewport.
Test only the default desktop screenshot.
Test long content and intrinsic sizing.
Test keyboard focus and zoomed text.

questions.explanation: Responsive validation needs a range of widths and content/accessibility conditions, not one screenshot.

questions.prompt: Which CSS change is a suitable baseline for a responsive image that should preserve its intrinsic ratio?

options.text: Set `width: 100vw` and fixed height
Set `max-width: 100%` and `height: auto`
Set `min-width: 100%` and `height: 1px`
Set `position: fixed`

questions.explanation: This allows the image to scale down to its container while preserving its intrinsic aspect ratio.

questions.prompt: Match each failure symptom to a likely investigation.

rows.label: Long text pushes a grid wider
Overlay is behind a neighboring section
Animation is uncomfortable for some users

questions.explanation: These symptoms commonly point to intrinsic sizing, stacking-context boundaries, and missing preference handling.

questions.prompt: Why can increasing a child's `z-index` fail inside a transformed card?

options.text: Transforms disable the `z-index` property everywhere
The child's position is always static
The transformed ancestor creates a stacking context that limits the child
CSS ignores z-index values above 100

questions.explanation: A transform can create a stacking context; descendants are ordered within it and cannot escape by using a larger z-index.

questions.prompt: What does `@supports selector(:has(img))` test?

options.text: Whether an image is currently loaded
Whether the document contains an image
Whether a container is wide enough
Whether the browser supports the tested selector syntax

questions.explanation: The `selector()` support condition queries selector support; it does not inspect runtime document matches.

questions.prompt: Which statements about modern feature fallbacks are correct?

options.text: A usable baseline can be declared before an enhancement.
`@supports` can gate a feature-dependent rule.
Every unsupported declaration disables the entire stylesheet.
The required browser support matrix is a product decision.

questions.explanation: CSS error recovery drops unsupported declarations; deliberate fallback patterns preserve baseline behavior.

questions.prompt: Which pair is a common safe fallback-first pattern for a modern layout feature?

options.text: A broadly supported declaration followed by an enhanced declaration
A modern declaration followed by an unconditional older declaration
Two contradictory declarations in separate IDs
Only a browser-specific prefix

questions.explanation: Declare a usable baseline first and layer a supported enhancement after it or within a feature query.

questions.prompt: Why should a team avoid putting `will-change: transform` on every element?

options.text: It permanently changes document semantics
It can consume resources and should be reserved for measured cases
It disables hardware compositing
It always forces a layout reflow

questions.explanation: `will-change` is a hint, not a free performance switch; widespread use can waste memory and rendering resources.

questions.prompt: Match each technique to its engineering purpose.
questions.explanation: Tokens, layers, and modifiers create separate contracts for values, cascade priority, and variants.

questions.prompt: What should a CSS architecture do with a one-off vendor override that repeatedly loses to specificity?

options.text: Add more IDs until it wins
Append `!important` to every property in the project
Place vendor and application rules in intentional cascade layers
Move the selector into an HTML comment

questions.explanation: Layering can establish priority by category and reduce specificity escalation.

questions.prompt: Which motion property pair is generally a better starting point for smooth UI transitions than animating layout dimensions?

options.text: `width` and `height`
`margin` and `top`
`grid-template-columns` and `padding`
`transform` and `opacity`

questions.explanation: Transform and opacity often avoid repeated layout work, though performance should still be measured in context.

questions.prompt: Which statements about motion and rendering are prudent?

options.text: Respect reduced-motion preferences.
Measure performance in the target experience.
Prefer transform/opacity for many small transitions when appropriate.
Treat `will-change` as a free global optimization.

questions.explanation: These choices balance accessibility and rendering cost; hints such as `will-change` require measured, selective use.

questions.prompt: What does `font-display: swap` prioritize during web-font loading?

options.text: Readable fallback text before the custom font is available
Waiting to show text until the font downloads
Disabling the custom font permanently
Replacing all system fonts with a generic face

questions.explanation: `swap` favors immediate text display with a fallback and swaps when the web font becomes ready.

questions.prompt: Match each output condition to its CSS mechanism.
questions.explanation: Use the matching media type, state pseudo-class, or token scope for each condition.

questions.prompt: Which viewport is a useful minimum-width test when checking for horizontal overflow?

options.text: Only a 4K desktop viewport
A narrow mobile viewport such as 320 CSS pixels
Only a print preview
A viewport with developer tools closed

questions.explanation: Small viewport testing exposes fixed widths, min-content overflow, and controls that do not adapt.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a design token and a component-specific literal?

options.text: A token is always a JavaScript variable
A literal always inherits
A token names a reusable design decision that can be changed centrally
A token bypasses the cascade

questions.explanation: Named custom properties can centralize design values and give themes/components a stable contract.

questions.prompt: Which practices reduce fragile cascade behavior in a growing codebase?

options.text: Use ancestor chains as the default component API.
Set an explicit layer order.
Keep selectors low-specificity where possible.
Treat `!important` as a deliberate exception.

questions.explanation: Layers and low-specificity component contracts reduce override coupling.

questions.prompt: A card looks correct at one desktop width but breaks in a narrow two-column page slot. Which test is most valuable?

options.text: Test only at the largest viewport
Check only the CSS file's line count
Disable all media queries
Render it in different container widths, including a narrow slot

questions.explanation: Component-level layouts should be tested in the widths they can actually occupy, not only at selected viewport sizes.

questions.prompt: What should a print stylesheet usually do with site navigation?

options.text: Hide nonessential navigation and preserve the primary content
Hide the article and keep navigation
Set every element to fixed positioning
Force every link to open in a new tab

questions.explanation: Print styles should emphasize the material being printed and remove nonessential interface chrome.

questions.prompt: Match each performance or quality decision to a sound practice.

columns.label: Use only for a measured case

questions.explanation: Measure instead of assuming, use rendering hints sparingly, and preserve a usable fallback.

questions.prompt: Which practice makes theme tokens easier to override locally?

options.text: Repeat the same value in every component selector
Define defaults in a low-specificity scope such as `:root` or a theme container
Use an ID for every token
Encode the value in pseudo-element text

questions.explanation: Centralized custom properties can be overridden at a theme or component boundary and inherited by descendants.

questions.prompt: Which statements about container queries are correct?

options.text: The queried container must be established for the query type.
A container query automatically changes the HTML structure.
A container query can make a component respond to its slot.
Viewport media queries and container queries have different inputs.

questions.explanation: Container queries adapt CSS to an ancestor's container context; they do not mutate document structure.

questions.prompt: A responsive navigation changes from horizontal to stacked. What is the correct reason to use a media query?

options.text: A particular item has a certain child
A color value fails parsing
The available viewport space changes the page-level navigation layout
The user focuses a button

questions.explanation: Viewport media queries are appropriate when a page-level layout should change with the viewport.

questions.prompt: What is a reliable way to confirm that a cascade fix solved the original issue?

options.text: Assume success because the CSS file saved
Raise specificity until the rule appears in source order
Remove unrelated declarations
Inspect computed styles and test the affected states and breakpoints

questions.explanation: Verify the winning computed declaration and rerun the state and viewport scenarios that exposed the issue.

questions.prompt: Which statements about generated content and semantics are correct?

options.text: Pseudo-elements can add decorative content.
Meaningful text should remain available in the document.
`content` creates a real HTML node in the DOM.
Generated content should not be the only source for essential instructions.

questions.explanation: Pseudo-element content is generated for rendering and should not replace essential semantic document content.

questions.prompt: Why should custom-property fallbacks be tested in the actual consuming property?

options.text: A token can exist yet yield a value invalid for that property's grammar
Fallbacks always override the declared token
Custom properties are resolved only at build time
Every CSS property accepts every token

questions.explanation: Custom properties store token streams; validation against the consuming property's grammar happens after substitution.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest engineering choice when adopting a CSS feature with uneven browser support?

options.text: Assume the newest browser feature is universal
Define the support requirement and provide a usable fallback or gate the enhancement
Use the feature only in an inline style
Hide the entire page when unsupported

questions.explanation: Feature support is a product requirement; use a baseline and a deliberate fallback or `@supports` gate.

questions.prompt: Which are useful production checks for a stylesheet change?

options.text: Inspect computed styles for the affected component.
Test relevant states and breakpoints.
Check contrast and keyboard focus.
Assume a passing build proves visual correctness.

questions.explanation: Build validation cannot replace browser, responsive, and accessibility checks.

questions.prompt: What is the most maintainable approach when a shared component needs a small visual variation?

options.text: Target it through a long chain of page-specific ancestors
Duplicate the whole stylesheet
Expose a documented custom-property or class modifier contract
Add an ID selector to every internal element

questions.explanation: A narrow component API makes intended variations explicit and avoids fragile selectors tied to page structure.
